facts.title: Named for the Titans
facts.text: Titanium was first recognized in 1791 by English clergyman and amateur mineralogist William Gregor, who found it in black sand near Manaccan, Cornwall. A few years later, German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth independently identified it and named it after the Titans of Greek mythology, the powerful children of Gaia and Uranus. The name nodded to its anticipated strength, even though pure metal would not be isolated for over a century.

facts.title: A century to purify
facts.text: Although discovered in the 1790s, reasonably pure titanium metal was not produced until 1910, when Matthew Hunter at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute reduced titanium tetrachloride with sodium. The metal stayed a laboratory curiosity until Luxembourg-born scientist William Kroll developed the magnesium-reduction Kroll process in 1940. That process is still the industrial standard today, which is one reason titanium remains relatively expensive.

facts.title: Strong as steel, far lighter
facts.text: Titanium has one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios of any structural metal. It is about as strong as many steels but roughly 45 percent lighter, with a density of about 4.5 grams per cubic centimeter versus around 7.9 for steel. This combination is why it is prized for jet engines, airframes, and high-performance bicycle frames.

facts.title: It heals its own armor
facts.text: Titanium resists corrosion because it instantly forms a thin, tough oxide layer when exposed to air or water. If this passive film is scratched, it re-forms in milliseconds wherever oxygen is present, protecting the metal underneath. This self-repairing shield lets titanium survive seawater and harsh chemicals that would rapidly eat away ordinary steel.

facts.title: The body accepts it
facts.text: Titanium is remarkably biocompatible, meaning the human body rarely rejects it. It can bond directly with living bone in a process called osseointegration, discovered by Swedish researcher Per-Ingvar Branemark in the 1950s. This makes it the material of choice for dental implants, hip and knee replacements, and surgical plates and screws.

facts.title: Hidden in your sunscreen
facts.text: The compound titanium dioxide is one of the whitest and most opaque substances known, so it is used as a pigment in paint, paper, plastics, and even toothpaste. It also absorbs and scatters ultraviolet light, which is why it is a common active ingredient in mineral sunscreens. Most titanium that is mined ends up as this dioxide rather than as the pure metal.

facts.title: Ninth most abundant element
facts.text: Titanium is the ninth most abundant element in Earth's crust, making up about 0.6 percent of it by mass. It is more common than familiar metals such as copper, nickel, and zinc, but it is never found as a free metal in nature. Instead it is locked inside minerals like rutile and ilmenite, and its difficult extraction keeps it costly despite its abundance.

facts.title: Moon rocks were rich in it
facts.text: Titanium is widespread in the cosmos and was found in surprising quantities in lunar samples returned by the Apollo missions. Some Moon basalts contain more than 10 percent titanium dioxide, far richer than typical Earth rocks of the same type. Astronomers also detect titanium oxide in the atmospheres of cool red stars, where it strongly shapes their spectra.

facts.title: Burns with a brilliant white
facts.text: While bulk titanium is hard to ignite, finely divided titanium powder or shavings burn fiercely with an intense white flame. It is one of the few elements that will keep burning in pure nitrogen gas, forming titanium nitride, and it also reacts directly with oxygen and even carbon at high temperatures. Because of this, titanium is used in fireworks and military flares to produce bright sparks.

facts.title: It turns rainbow colors
facts.text: When titanium is anodized, an electric current thickens its oxide layer to a precisely controlled depth. Light reflecting off this transparent film interferes with itself, producing vivid blues, purples, and golds with no dyes or paints involved. Jewelers and artists exploit this effect, and the colors are determined purely by the oxide thickness, which depends on the voltage used.
